In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of obesity, as measured by body mass index (BMI), on the carotid artery intima-media thickness (CIMT) in adults with primary hypertension in Nigeria.
the effects of body mass index on the thickness of the carotid intimal media.
the effects of obesity and body composition on cardiovascular disease (CVD) in the general population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

BMI is not an accurate measure of body fat and that the BMI should not be used to assess the health risks associated with obesity in the Nigerian population, especially in those with hypertension and diabetes.
the use of body mass index as a measure of obesity is not a reliable indicator of cardiovascular risk in the general population of Nigeria.
obesity is associated with an increase in CVD and that the relationship between obesity and CVD is mediated by hypertension.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found that BMI is associated with CVD risk, but that the association between BMI and CVD risk is not linear, and that the association is modified by sex, race, and age.
we found that the prevalence of hypertension in the adult Nigerian population was 33% and that 50% of the hypertensive population was unaware of their disease status.
we have shown that the body mass index (BMI) is a significant determinant of carotids intima-media thickness (CIMT) and that it is more so in the hypertensives than in the normotensives.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we can use a single, simple, inexpensive, noninvasive measure, the carotid intimal-media thickness, to identify patients at high risk of cardiovascular events and who might benefit from more aggressive therapy.
body fat is a better predictor of carotid artery intima-media thickness than body mass index.
the association between body mass index (BMI) and carotid intimal media thickness (IMT) is not linear, and that the association may vary by sex.
